title: The 50/72 Rule — Writing Clear Commit Subject Lines
learning_objectives: Apply the 50-character subject line limit and understand why it matters
Write commit subjects in imperative mood correctly
Follow subject line capitalization rules and avoid trailing periods
Identify and fix vague or over-broad commit descriptions
Distinguish good from bad subject lines at a glance
outline: Quick review: Conventional Commits structure (type, scope, subject)
The 50-character rule: why 50 and what happens past 72
The 'if applied' test: a mental shortcut for imperative mood
Subject line rules: capitalize first word, no trailing period, be specific
Hands-on: Rewrite 5 bad commit subject lines for Helm

helm_context.feature: Professional commit history for Helm repository
helm_context.deliverable: 5 improved commit subject lines applied to real Helm commits

criteria: All subject lines are 50 characters or fewer
Imperative mood used correctly in every subject
Appropriate Conventional Commits type prefix on each
Subjects are specific — no vague 'fix', 'update', or 'changes'
First word capitalized, no trailing period

resources.title: How to Write a Git Commit Message (Chris Beams)

professor_constraints: Keep the CC format review to 2-3 minutes max — learner completed L01
Use Helm-specific examples (tasks, time blocks, Google Calendar sync) not CatchBook
Provide exactly 5 bad commit subject lines for the hands-on exercise
Show git log --oneline output to demonstrate how subject lines appear in practice
Address the 'what if my change is complex' concern: that's what commit bodies are for (covered in L03)

metadata.note: Redesigned from 90-min lesson covering full commit message craft. Now focused solely on subject lines. Bodies/footers → L03, atomic commits/amend → L04.
